title: The first question (Berakhot 2a)
hook: the whole Talmud opens by asking from when the evening Shema may be said

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened a page of Talmud and found it starts on page two. Your line was there's no page one. Did you start something without waiting for the perfect start? Day two hundred seventy-one.

If you were writing the most important book of your people, how would you open it? Maybe with God. Maybe with creation, or the meaning of life. The Talmud, the giant library of Jewish law and argument, opens with a question that sounds almost like a text to a friend. From what time can you say the evening Shema? That's it. That's the first line. No grand speech, no introduction. Just a practical question about tonight. Today we sit with that question, because it turns out to hold a whole way of seeing time.
screen: `THE MOST IMPORTANT BOOK.` → `HOW DOES IT OPEN?` → `FROM WHAT TIME, TONIGHT?`

segments.voice: The Shema is the line at the heart of Jewish prayer, Hear, O Israel, said morning and evening. The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So the rabbis asked: lying down begins when, exactly? The Mishnah answers: from the time the priests go in to eat their holy food, at nightfall. And until when? Three answers. Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night. The sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until the first light of dawn. And then a story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home late from a wedding feast, past midnight, and said: we haven't said the Shema yet. He told them: if dawn hasn't come, you still can, and you still should. Then the Talmud asks its own question about the question. Why start with evening, and not morning? One answer: because the verse itself says lying down first, then rising up. Another: because in the story of creation, the evening comes first. "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." That's the order the tradition follows: a Jewish day, Shabbat and every holiday, begins in the evening, not at midnight or sunrise. The day starts in the dark and grows toward light. So the first question of the Talmud isn't small at all. It asks you to notice the exact moment one day becomes the next, and to meet it with words.
screen: `WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN.` · `THREE ANSWERS: WATCH, MIDNIGHT, DAWN.` · `THE SONS COME HOME LATE.` · `EVENING COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `WHEN DOES EVENING START?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own evening. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think back over the last few days. When does your evening really begin? When you close the laptop? When the kids are asleep? When the light outside changes color, or when you finally put your phone face down? Picture that moment. Now picture meeting it on purpose, with one breath or one line you care about. If you pray, it could be the Shema. If not, it could simply be noticing: the day is turning. The bell holds the time.
The first question. The Talmud opens by asking from when the evening Shema may be said, and answers: from nightfall, because in the Torah the evening comes first.
Your line: when does evening start. Tonight, catch the moment your day turns into evening, and mark it with one quiet breath. Day two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Observant Jews say the Shema in the evening prayer (Maariv) after nightfall and again at bedtime, and every Jewish day, including Shabbat and the holidays, begins at sundown.

trapdoor: what you thought: a technical question about a prayer schedule.
what it means: the Talmud's first question teaches that a day begins at evening.
what a scholar hears: the Gemara asks why the Mishnah starts with evening, and answers from Deuteronomy 6:7 and from Genesis 1:5, where evening comes first.

notes: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 is paraphrased: Rabbi Eliezer (until the end of the first watch), the sages (until midnight), Rabban Gamliel (until dawn), and the story of his sons returning from a wedding feast.
The two reasons for starting with evening (the order of Deuteronomy 6:7; the order of Genesis 1:5) both appear on Berakhot 2a; confirm the framing.
The sages' midnight limit is described in the Mishnah as a fence; the script simplifies this. A Keeper may want it mentioned.
Check JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 6:7 and Genesis 1:5.

Review fix: the opening time (from when the priests enter to eat their terumah) is the Mishnah's anonymous first statement, not Rabbi Eliezer's; Rabbi Eliezer gives only the end of the first watch. Script corrected.
The exact moment the day turns (sunset vs. nightfall, bein hashmashot) is itself debated; the teach now says 'begins in the evening' rather than tying the reason to Genesis as settled.
